subsubtopic: GATINEAU PARK-ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXCHANGE OF LANDS WITH QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this almost spring day I have an announcement of some interest. I wish to announce that the federal government and the government of Quebec have agreed to a mutually advantageous administrative exchange of lands contained within the national capital region, almost entirely within Gatineau Park. The province of Quebec will transfer to the federal government approximately 12,500 wilderness acres it still holds within the western confines of the park. This will enable the National Capital Commission, which manages the park, to plan, control and administer the park as an entity from the standpoints of both recreation and conservation. Generally speaking, the western end of the park is being maintained as a wilderness area.
In exchange, for the transfer of this large acreage by the province of Quebec to the federal government we are transferring to Quebec the administration of some land in the southern end of the park adjacent to Hull, and some non-park land for rights of way and road widening. Altogether, the lands being transferred by the federal
government constitute some 255 acres of urban-related land.
The parcels of parkland being transferred to Quebec are to be used exclusively for educational, cultural, recreational and other purposes in the public interest. Quebec has agreed to declare Gatineau park a game reserve and to restrict mining exploration within the park.
I might add that this agreement I am announcing brings to a successful conclusion negotiations which I am informed have been proceeding on and off for a dozen years.

subsubtopic: GATINEAU PARK-ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXCHANGE OF LANDS WITH QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on this spring day I want to echo the feeling of complete acceptance of this agreement and to say how pleased we are to hear the minister's announcement. We have always felt that Gatineau Park was really a national park in the fullest sense of the word, although it is an adornment particularly to the national capital area. It is pleasing to us to hear that arrangements are being made to develop the park as it has been slated to be developed, under one jurisdiction. To put our feelings correctly, may I say that we greet this announcement with the same joy that we would greet an announcement that there had been successful negotiations with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec with respect to the creation of a rapid transit system for the national capital area.

subsubtopic: GATINEAU PARK-ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXCHANGE OF LANDS WITH QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may comment very briefly on the minister's announcement I should like to say it is certainly very pleasant to hear some good news from the minister.

speechtext: For a change.

subsubtopic: GATINEAU PARK-ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXCHANGE OF LANDS WITH QUEBEC
speechtext: The completion of this agreement between the federal and the Quebec authorities will without doubt result in administrative benefits for the new land areas concerned. The pity is as the minister has said, that has taken 10 to 12 years to complete the agreement. subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CHAPLAINS NOT TO BE EMPLOYEES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-160, to amend the Penitentiary Act (religious freedom).

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CHAPLAINS NOT TO BE EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CHAPLAINS NOT TO BE EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under section 10 of the Penitentiary Act at the moment people who are employed as prison chaplains are in fact peace officers or policemen and are under the statutory authority of the warden and the Commissioner of Penitentiaries. The purpose of this bill is to reflect the view that it is inappropriate for a chaplain also to be a policeman and, accordingly, to provide that chaplains, while retaining all rights of access to penitentiaries and communications with inmates, shall not be employees as such under the Penitentiary Act, and thus be in a better position to fulfil their important role within a penitentiary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like today, as a result of a previous agreement, to continue and conclude the speech which I began on March 7 concerning the Standing Orders and the procedure governing us as well as the motion of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) aimed at enabling the Committee on Procedure and Organization to carry out its review of our Standing Orders.
Mr. Speaker, at the very beginning of my speech on Wednesday last, I explained rather briefly why we are dissatisfied with such and such a point and I raised, as you know, some special problems.
I would like, since I have that opportunity, to conclude my speech by making some specific proposals. As for the oral question period, Mr. Speaker, we are embittered and frustrated, not because we do not get the floor, even if on some days we get it more often than on others. Speaker, the matter is beyond your control, since you have to deal with the influx of supplementaries.
Mr. Speaker, some colleagues wanted the oral question period to be extended. We believe that a 40-minute period is sufficient, provided it is well used. Even if we had an 80-minute oral question period, it would still be 80 minutes of clowning of we do not change the procedure.
Mr. Speaker, if we stick to the same method during the oral question period, and extend it, it will be 80 minutes of torture for you and for us. I believe we should consider, in the Committee on Procedure and Organization, serious

March 9, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure
reforms as to the proceedure during the oral question period.
During the meetings held by the Committee on Procedure and Organization and during that trip to Westminster, it was often proposed to proceed from now as follows: any member wishing to ask an oral question would give notice of it to the minister concerned who could thus reply in a more serious way. On the one hand, it would improve answers and the political aspect of our question period would be removed, while on the other hand, it would inable the Chair to put aside questions that lead to clowning, waste time or have but one reason, namely to get the member's name in Handsard. At any event, we are ready to consider most seriously the proposal concerning notices during the oral question period.
But we shall be more watchful in connection with the famous supplementary questions. Mr. Speaker, after a serious examination of the result of the oral question period, we have come to the conclusion-and we have statistics in support of that-that more time is given during the 40-minute oral question period to supplementary questions than to first questions.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that hon. members should be responsible enough to recognize the need to abolish, and I repeat abolish, the practice of supplementary questions.
We propose that a member be allowed to ask a question and even a supplementary to his own question. Then, another member could be recognized, but not under the pretext of asking a supplementary question.
Mr. Speaker, that is our position. Of course we don't have your experience and knowledge although we would like to very much, but in spite of our shortcomings in that regard, we intend to fight in all sincerity to put a stop to supplementary questions.
What happens? It happened today, it happened yesterday, it happens every day; there is an oral questions period.
Mr. Speaker, that is why we hate that period. The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) rises to ask a question and then 10, 15, 20, 30 or 40 backbenchers want to take the opportunity to ask supplementaries. If a serious examination is made, which I hope the committee will do, not only of the number but also of the content of these questions, one will note that very often their content has no relation to the initial question and as the question period progresses, the further the final supplementary is from the initial subject; as Speaker, you cannot refuse to recognize a member. The backbenchers who have a question on another subject cannot put it since the Chair must deal exhaustively with a matter before going on to another one.
Mr. Speaker, our suggestion comes to this: First, the question period is long enough as it is; second, an equal distribution of time between opposition parties must be made on the first round. We do not accept and we will not accept, Mr. Speaker, to go on putting up with the same ridiculous system under which the first question asked by the Speaker of our party practically comes at the end of

the first half of the oral question period, and this because of the supplementaries.
This situation is injust and antiparliamentary in that it does not equally respect the rights of each party on the first round. As for the first round, we seriously consider that the party leader or his delegate should be allowed to ask a first question, and then that a maximum of two or three supplementaries be asked on the subject. Thus, members of our party would be more quickly recognized. Then, Mr. Speaker, no supplementaries should be allowed from anyone other than the member who asked the question initially and only one supplementary should be granted if the member deems it necessary.
Since any procedural reform is made on an experimental basis-we must admit it since the House rules are continuously revised-this formula should be voluntarily accepted and made part of the rules so that the Chair will no longer have to do the thankless task of exhausting a subject before going on to another.
If hon. members were not so respectful of the Chair surely all those who are in our situation, and there are many, would protest. Everyone knows that those critics are not aimed at the Chair but at the system which turned the question period into a joke for the public in the House at that time and into a shame for the Chair because it is caught in this situation. I am saying it because your politeness and dignity will keep you from saying so, Mr. Speaker; it is our duty to say so ourselves and for the hon. members it is a source of continued and daily frustrations.
I sincerely hope, in the name of my party, that the proposal to eliminate the supplementary questions will be seriously examined to give new value to the question period which fundamentally is an excellent initiative based on excellent principles in that sense that current questions are raised daily and thus the government has to take position every day on his actions as a government, and it enables the opposition to check on those actions and to get information.
I think that with the implementation of Standing Order 39(5), which permits the Speaker to order that non-urgent questions be put on the order paper, we can have again question periods worthy of the name.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in connection again with Standing Order 43 I stated in my speech of last Wednesday that it was abnormal that the Chair be required to get involved to accept or reject a motion under section 26 because under this seciton it is incumbent on the Chair, which has been given notice, to decide as to the national importance or urgency of a question. I think that if Mr. Speaker is requested, under Standing Orders, to get involved and rule on the urgency of a question, I do not see why the other members, when they refuse their unanimous consent under Standing Order 43, should not have also to identify themselves and to get involved as the Chair does under Standing Order 26.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we would really move in the direction anticipated when we tried to amend Standing Order 26. Therefore, we are suggesting that each time fewer than five hon. members refuse unanimous consent, they be identified in order to clarify the official report of the
March 9, 1973

House of Commons, and that those who hide behind anonymity to refuse leave to move a motion under Standing Order 43 from now on be compelled to take their responsibilities and to identifythemselves, as the Chair does with such dignity and ability when making a decision on a motion moved under Standing Order 26.
Mr. Speaker, in this debate I wanted to make another remark: since entering the House in 1968, I have been trying to take interest in the procedure of the House of Commons, to learn the Standing Orders as much as I can. However, the task is not easy. The reason is that the documentation concerning the procedure is published in English.
Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms available for our guidance is an outdated book. The only decent book on the subject is the last edition of May's Parliamentary Practice, published in 1971. Now, that edition is exclusively in English.
Mr. Speaker, the government having one day recognized the right of each hon. member to speak in the House in his mother tongue, the importance of providing simultaneous translation and of publishing the Standing Orders of the House of Commons as well as the Parliamentary Rules and Forms in French, I consider that it would be sensible for the House of Commons, even at the price of increasing its budget, which should be recommended by the Committee on Procedure and Organization, to have the last edition of Sir Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice translated into French, in order to prevent the French-speaking hon. members from being caught off guard when it is a matter of knowing about precedents. That would be a positive step which would allow all hon. members, whatever their language may be, to really understand those citations.
I would like to make another suggestion concerning the work of committees. In the speech he made the President of the Privy Council quoted very interesting figures-even surprising figures-to illistrate a comparison between the work of committees and the work of the House. It is found that the work of parliamentary committees increases from one session to the other to the point of becoming a nightmare for all parties and all members.
We have looked into the matter. We met, studied the problem and came up with certain findings. First, committee meetings should not be held when the House is sitting. That means that it would be suitable for the Committee on Procedure and Organization-since its terms of reference are rather broad-to consider the possibility of scheduling the week differently in order to allow the same subject matter to be examined in committee and in the House at two different times.
We would also like to make another suggestion to give the House more time and allow hon. members who wish to introduce a bill or a motion to really participate in the business of the House. We know that at the present time private members' hour comes up four times a week and after the total of 40 hours has been reached there are only two hours a week after that on Thursdays and Fridays. We would like to propose that private members hour be abolished during the week in order to allow the House to devote more time to its business; furthermore, we would
Standing Orders and Procedure
like to have Fridays-except for the question period- devoted exclusively to private members' business.
So a good many hon. members could devote Fridays to their private affairs. On the other hand, hon. members who live far away could spend more time with constituents in their ridings, whereas they now have very little time to meet people, what with travelling back and forth between Ottawa and their residence. Hon. members who are not directly interested in private members' business could do what they what during that day as these motions are normally not put to the vote.
A third proposal concerning private members' business or committee work is that-especially when the government is in minority-the government could do much more work more quickly in the Committee of the Whole, even if the rules of the House must be changed, because it would be given more work. Let us change the rules of the House while giving the Committee of the Whole the opportunity to play a more efficient part in the House.
For some years we have tended increasingly to keep the parliamentary committees busy. The speech of the President of the Privy Council contains ample proof of this. I wonder why we could not, not necessarily put an end to committee work, but pick out certain very important bills from the government's list so that they can come before the House of Commons more quickly.
The advantage of a Committee of the Whole over a parliamentary committee is that all the latter can do is to approve a bill, hear evidence and then approve the decision of the House. It can amend a bill, but this happen very seldom. When a committee has reported and recommended that the bill be passed, the House of Commons has to study the bill all over again. A Committee of the Whole has the advantage of cutting out one whole stage. Clauses of a bill are studied and approved simultaneously, the report is made, and that is that.
I think that, in view of how important it is to speed up our proceedings, we should certainly look into the possibility of doing more as the Committee of the Whole.
Also, Mr. Speaker, in order to increase efficiency and improve individual members' contributions, the government should previously, as early on as possible, supply a list of the bills it intends to table at the opening of a session. The government should, in my opinion, give us a list of bills that they are ready to table, prior to each session; that would enable members to carry out research in their own time rather than in haste, and to prepare well-documented speeches rather than well-padded ones, and would thus improve the quality of debates. It seems to me only right that members should have copies of bills sooner in advance than at present, when a day or two is the rule.
These bills could then be put in order of priority and, under an agreement between House leaders, I believe that our proceedings could be speeded up, according to the experience we would have had.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks that I wished to make. My last point relates to a reform that has been made in the British Parliament. In the British House of

March 9, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure Commons, it is understood that second reading of a bill should not last more than a day, unless the House decides otherwise. This is not laid down in the rules of the House, but in view of the pressure of parliamentary business today, the principle has the mutual agreement of the government and opposition parties. It is one of the conventions or "gentlemen's agreements" governing the schedule of parliamentary debates. I wonder whether it might not be appropriate to try or adopt a similar policy in this House, namely to shorten consideration on second reading since, at any rate, one can see that in view of increased parliamentary business in committees, second reading of a bill has become of minor importance and is almost a formal procedure.
As the work done in parliamentary committees has been increased and that it is also intended to increase the work of the Committee of the Whole-this is obvious since the beginning of the present session-I wonder whether it might not be appropriate to come to a mutual agreement in order to cut down the time devoted to consideration of a bill on second reading to one day, for instance, so that there will not be any duplication.
What disappoints me most, Mr. Speaker, in this House, is the fact that we are constantly doing the same work. First reading of a bill is a formal procedure, second reading is a waste of time; consideration in Committee of the Whole or in a parliamentary committee must still be done. Our approach is piecemeal. We hear witnesses and then we make a thorough study of the question. At the report stage the House of Commons does over again from the beginning the study of the bill made at the committee level. Hon. members who were on the committee again take the floor. Then, after the report stage, the third reading is the most important step because it is final. Therefore, I do not see why the other parties could not do as we do and agree to reduce to one day the time spent on second reading so as to save more time.
We should not forget, Mr. Speaker, that each member had been elected according to a democratic process, to work efficiently. Moreover, we should not forget that the rules and procedure are nothing more than tools and not an end in themselves and that a tool is useful only to the extent that we use it to our advantage. We are not here to serve the rules; indeed, the rules must be our servant.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, this party is prepared to co-operate at any time to facilitate the business of the House, to make it more efficient, more modern and more active; but we also expect the other opposition and government parties to be more serious when they study the procedures so that each member be entitled to give his own views and that the House not be crippled by protracted debates.
I know that we will reach that objective, Mr. Speaker, if we show some willingness. Then we will have some results if we make a special effort with respect to the oral question period, a matter which happens to be the central issue right now.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say again that our fight will bear on the oral question period and that we will certainly urge very strongly that supplementary questions be abolished.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you must be delighted to be listening to a debate this Friday afternoon on a matter as dear to your heart as the rules and proceedings of this House. It will give you a great deal to ruminate about, I hope, in the course of what I hope will be a relaxing and pleasant weekend.
The comments that have been made so far on Wednesday, and again today, have contributed I think a great number of positive suggestions which, I am sure, will be seriously considered by the committee and, I trust, as well by all members of the House. I think is has become transparently obvious in a little more than the two months that parliament has been sitting that we have some particularly difficult problems to grapple with in terms of the effective procedures of this House.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), when he was speaking in opening the debate on Wednesday made two comments that he had heard when visiting parliament at Westminster. He said that over and over again those who were commenting on the situation with regard to the procedures of the British House of Commons said that they had discovered two things: one is that there were only 365 days in the year, and second, that after a certain amount of discussion enough was enough. I think that that is something with which all members would agree, but how we resolve the many intricate questions that balance off the competing interests and necessary requirements for this parliament is a most difficult exercise.
As the President of the Privy Council remarked, we are getting into an increasing progression of examinations with respect to the procedures of the House. I think he said that in the first 30 years of this parliament back in the last century there was really no re-examination of the basic rules that had been established, but that with greater and greater frequency up until the past decade we have examined and re-examined the rules of the House.
I do not think that this should concern us, and certainly it does not concern me. In fact, I would be disturbed if it were otherwise. I am, after all, a Progressive Conservative and perhaps, if I may say this without any particular label being attached to it, I think the approach one must take in examining the rules is a progressive and a conservative one. I believe there are basic elements which quite obviously must be conserved in the functioning of the House and in the protection that it affords to individuals as well as to the total society of this country. I think we have to recognize increasingly that parliament is faced with a vastly changing and, might I say, an accelerating change of situation with respect to our responsibilities and with respect to the country which we seek to serve.
I will not spend long talking about how we should deal with estimates, but I think it is important to realize how difficult this can be. If I remember correctly, the strong feeling that came from many members of the House when we decided to make a major change in our rules was that the debates that had taken place, literally since the beginning in the House, on estimates were increasingly being frustrated by the fact that when we were dealing with the estimates of expenditures of a particular department the debates often tended to fly off in all directions. For one

March 9, 1973

reason or another, because of either a member's particular constituency interests or some momentary distraction, essential questions and essential information with respect to a government department was not adequately dealt with. I say this regardless of which government happened to be in power at any particular time.
There was a sense of real frustration for Members of Parliament generally, and I think for the general public, that we were really not getting into the departments in a detailed way, that we were not probing to a sufficient extent so that the fullest possible amount of public stewardship could be exercised with respect to government expenditures. Therefore a majority decision was taken. The decision was taken to move the examination of the estimates from the Committee of the Whole into a growing number of standing committees. It was felt that there Members of Parliament would be free, not just for one or two hours, but literally for days and weeks, to examine not only the ministers-and ministers of course are fundamentally responsible-but all of the battery of officials who have such an important role to play in the administration of government business. From a theoretical standpoint I do not think anybody could seriously question that decision. But what has been the result in practice? It has been twofold.
In the first instance, there has been a tremendous number of committee meetings. There has been a tremendous increase at least in the amount of information put on the record. We might well ask whether or not the way in which that information has been presented, and the completeness of that information, would still be regarded as sufficient. I personally feel, from the time I have spent on a variety of standing committees, that there is still much room for improvement in the eliciting and the presentation of detailed information in committees. But further than that, we have found two structural problems. First since we have not yet arrived at a systematic arrangement for committees within the last few years we have found that the way in which committees have been examining estimates has been very erratic, to say the least.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, I think of the meeting that took place last year of the Committee on Health and Welfare, which is the committee also responsible for examining the estimates of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. How those two are connected is somewhat of a mystery to me, but I suppose it results from the fact that our standing committees still do not match the various departments of government.
As a result of our having gone in a thorough manner through previous estimates under the health and welfare umbrella, we were then faced with the necessity of processing the estimates of the whole Department of Corporate and Consumer Affairs within a matter of hours, with just the briefest and skimpiest kind of examination. As I recall it, the minister made an opening statement. There was little more than one hour left in which a few questions could be asked and then, as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) himself suggested, the guillotine fell because under our rules, once we reach the end of May, all estimates are considered to have been passed by the committees. I think all hon. members will agree that that is a most unsatisfactory, in fact I would
Standing Orders and Procedure
say most irresponsible, way for use to deal with a basic responsibility, namely, our stewardship of the public purse.
Further to that, the usefulness which parliament achieved over the years, going well back into the last century, of being able to exercise final control over the expenditure of public money by its granting of supply, has well nigh been lost under our present rules arrangement. I think it is clear to all members of the House that we will have to look very closely at, and deal much more effectively with, the whole question of the granting of supply and the final right of parliament to grant supply, because if there is anything we can seriously criticize in the most recent rules revision it is the fact that parliament was emasculated with respect to its control over the expenditure of public funds. I think all hon. members will have to ensure that, when rules and recommendations come from the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, this serious fault in the present rules is corrected.
I have risen today, Mr. Speaker, not to speak principally about the difficulty with estimates but to put before you the problems that have arisen with respect to the growing pre-occupation with the effective functioning of the question period. I do this because I have long been a devotee of the question period, as you will recall, Sir. You, Sir, may be somewhat disappointed by the fact that I have not been nearly as active in seeking Your Honour's eye in this session as I have in previous sessions, although it may be that you are not so disappointed. In fact, I know that some of my colleagues to my left and even to my right are somewhat pleased that I have chosen to contribute one less body to the daily forest of figures attempting to engage Your Honour's attention. However, we have gotten into a very serious situation with the question period. I, for one, am extremely glad that we will shortly give the question period very effective scrutiny in this committee and, I presume, at a later date in a more general way in this House, when that committee makes its recommendations.
The President of the Privy Council, when he was speaking on Wednesday and dealing with this same problem, expressed concern about the way in which questions and answers had stopped being questions and answers, and had moved more towards being mini-debates or, to use my own phrase, had become more of a form of political posturing on one side of the chamber or the other. I think that his concern about this is valid. I think he would agree with me that all questions and answers, because of the very nature of this place, will carry a political edge with them. If they do not, then the individuals who are providing one or the other are really not effectively fulfilling their function. But I am more than a little concerned that the President of the Privy Council feels that a simple extension of the question period will not alone be a sufficient remedy. Putting it just in those terms there may be some validity to his concern, and I notice that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) made somewhat the same comment. But I think we have to recognize a physical situation when it exists.
In the adjustment of our rules during the last ten years we have moved to restrict increasingly the time of the

March 9, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure question period. Question periods, in a way, are the thermometer of parliament itself. Question periods get to be contentious, disputatious, active, vibrant simply because parliament, in any general political situation, is itself of that nature. It would be the strangest possible world indeed if we were to have, in the present particular situation, a question period where, after ten, 15 or 20 minutes, it was decided to go on to other business. The wonder may well be, given our present situation, that there are not more people either attempting to ask or answer questions during that period. It is a well known fact that in the last parliament, which had 50 less members on the opposition side, there was hardly a time, certainly within my memory during those three or four years, when we reached the end of the question period that Your Honour was still not trying to recognize about half a dozen members seeking to be recognized for the purpose of asking questions.
Now, we are in a situation where the opposition side has grown by 50 per cent. Indeed, I would argue in a de facto sense that it has grown by 100 per cent. It is not only that there are 50 more members to Your Honour's left in this parliament but it is also true that the attendance and concern for recognition, both combined, have grown by at least another 50 per cent to 100 per cent. We know, when it comes to the matter of voting, that we have achieved some unusually high voting figures during the first two months of this parliament. Perhaps we will not see soon again the 95 per cent batting average that we have recently displayed with respect to vote participation, but that same kind of participation has been and is a factor in the day to day question period.
We all know that this particular parliament is fragile and quite likely will be short lived. And members, whether they are new members, of whom we have roughly 100, or whether they are veterans of more than one parliament, realize there will be a very short space between the election of last fall and the next election in the close, foreseeable future. Therefore, no matter how long the question period is, it still will not be long enough. But that is not just the sole question. I think we will have to achieve an acceptable length of question period that can be adjusted somewhat depending on the realities of any particular parliament. Certainly, the reality of this parliament is that 40 minutes are not long enough, and I do not see that much of an argument can be made on either side of the House that 40 minutes should be long enough.
How should we do it? I think, quite frankly, that on an average basis the question period should last 60 minutes. I hope Your Honour will not shudder at the thought of having to put up with that. As a member of the opposition,
I want to say to Your Honour that I appreciate the way that at times you have been able not to see the clock. Today, you were kind enough to extend that brief period at the sufferance of all members so that individual members could be recognized, but I do not want to put Your Honour in the difficult position of having to make that kind of subjective decision too frequently. I do not think, however, that we should lose the virtue, and I believe there was some element of virtue in it, of what was in existence in this parliament for almost the first 90 years when there was no time limit on question period.

Lest hon. members believe that I am now going to argue for a unlimited question period, I am not. We need an equitable time which I regard as one hour, but I think that parliament has to be able to adapt to the realities of its political situation and there should be an additional safety valve to allow for this. I propose that on occasion, perhaps a designated day of the week, when at the end of the question period an hon. member requests additional time, if ten members stand to concur with this request, then additional time should be granted. I do not know how radical this will seem to some of my more conservative friends or how conservative to some of my more progressive friends, but I suggest that more flexibility must be built into the question period.
Some members may argue that the question period is already too great a part of the parliamentary day. To them I would point out that at the present time it occupies something like 12 per cent of the day, and 75 per cent or 85 per cent is left for other things such as government business. If we are looking for some greater sense of discipline and stewardship in the use of time, we should consider seriously suggestions such as that made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) about unlimited time for almost everything else. There is no coming to grips on such things as say, the time of debates to establish parliamentary committees, one of which took four days recently, or debate on second reading which goes on for a long period and other such matters. There are time limits on the budget debate and the Address in Reply debate. I think it is unrealistic to believe that parliament can function effectively without some effective discipline on our time. But there must be greater flexibility with regard to the probing that is part and parcel of the question period and it need not be unworkable.
The suggestion of the President of the Privy Council that we might make more use of notice in the question period has some merit. By tradition this has been an informal thing and has not been used to any great extent. I think there is a greater problem, however, in the use of the order paper. The President of the Privy Council referred to this briefly when he said that the written questions on the order paper had "gone out of sight". He has been around here longer than I, so perhaps one's vision depends on what one regards as the fundamental measure. He listed 1,420 questions of which 329 had been answered, but I would not think that was a great number of questions for the number of members we have. We need not be unduly alarmed about the need for expansion when we compare it to the expansion of government itself. We are dealing with close to $20 billion of public money and expending it through almost 30 departments and 300,000 employees, so the 264 members must try to do their job as extensively and resourcefully as possible. It would be a mistake to deny the possibility for vigilance.
The hon. President of the Privy Council would agree that there is a need to distinguish between parliament and government. Parliament is not the government; it is a forum, the nation's public forum where the rights of citizens are protected and government actions can be examined, ratified or rejected and where nationally accepted laws are put forward and passed. If this is to be done effectively, the number of questions will be increased. I was glad to hear the President of the Privy Council say
March 9, 1973

that he was working to improve the machinery of government in order to facilitate responses. Members will not feel like resorting to written questions if they are going to lie dormant on the order paper for months, not just days or weeks. While the President of the Privy Council took some pride in the fact that 329 questions have been answered, I must point out that more than 1,000 have not. It could well be that some of these questions need to be put in a more responsible way so that they can be answered in a reasonably short time. If we are not going to provide better machinery to deal with them and the production of papers, then obviously the frustrations will not be restricted to the oral question period.
I was glad to hear the President of the Privy Council suggest that guidelines will be drawn up for requests for the production of papers with the possibility of debate and further examination by a committee. This is an area which needs to be upgraded. The rules should be agreed upon and made known to all members of the House with regard to the presentation of government reports. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) suggested the other day, I suspect that a good many of the ground rules, formal and informal, are concerned with the security of the government rather than the security of the state.
I have left open the assumption that there is a real necessity that all governments accept, that the public has a right and a need to know.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps this would be an appropriate time to call it one o'clock.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
Perhaps a good lunch has fortified us. I want to mention a couple of issues that are related to the question period. A moment or two before we rose at one o'clock I was referring to the need for written questions to be answered rapidly. I also concede that there is much wisdom in one of the suggestions made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), namely that we should look at the form in which written questions are put so members will have the right to expect that, when written questions are submitted, they will be answered within a reasonable period of time. This will lead, I submit, to broadened and more relevant participation in the proceedings of the House on the part of hon. members.
With regard to starred questions, I think the committee should look at the usefulness of starred questions. I am
Standing Orders and Procedure
not sure of the original reasons for the introduction of starred questions. To me, there is attached to starred questions a somewhat odd quality in that they do not perform any function more useful than that of ordinary, written questions. Certainly, in the last few weeks we have seen some examples of time consuming, extended answers to starred questions. Perhaps we ought to consider the suggestion brought forward by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) from time to time, a suggestion which, so far, has not been incorporated in the accepted practices of this House, namely, that some time limitation be imposed with regard to answers to starred questions. Starred questions, if they are to be useful at all, should occupy an intermediate position between questions asked during the oral question period, when answers are given immediately, and written questions, the answers to which may take a few days, or even one week, to be brought forward. I think the 48 hour limit suggested by the right hon. member is workable, and should be considered by the committee.
So far in this debate the question of adjournment proceedings being used for the purpose of answering questions has not been raised. However, I would point out to Your Honour that at the present time there is a list of some 70 questions awaiting to be dealt with on the adjournment debate. If one computes by very simple mathematics that we have, when all is working well, roughly nine opportunities a week to present these questions, and then divide 70 by nine, it would show that something like two months would pass before we reached the end of the present list.
Now, we know that special debates, opposition days and other things occasionally intervene, so that not often do we in fact get nine opportunities a week to put these questions. Therefore, the time frame for the answering of questions becomes even more extended. What has happened, then, is that these questions have already backed up to a considerable degree. These are the questions which Your Honour has suggested are more appropriate for the adjournment debate than for extensive discussion during the course of the regular question period.
If I may just refer to a few of the questions listed to date, it will give Your Honour an idea of the kind of unworkable situation we have. There is one question submitted by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) dated January 15 in which he seeks information about a meeting of federal and provincial finance ministers. Mr. Speaker, if that meeting is the one to which I think he refers, it took place at the end of January. My hon. friend will have to re-word his question, obviously, so that he can talk about future meetings of that sort. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) placed a question on January 19 concerning veterans' allowances. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is well known that this matter has been the subject of a bill since that time and is now before this House for consideration. Another hon. friend of mine, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), on January 25 put a question on the subject of cost of drugs to senior citizens, a subject which was to be raised at the Conference on Old Age Pensions. Well that conference was held a month or a month and a half ago.

March 9, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) asked a question on January 30 seeking better information on the Local Initiatives Program. This program is rapidly approaching its expiration date. Finally, and perhaps the most bizarre example of the situation in which we now find ourselves on February 2 the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), put down a question on the subject of the income tax forms and the difficulty some people are having in getting help with their forms through the use of the Zenith telephone number. Mr. Speaker, by the time the hon. member gets an answer the whole subject will likely be academic, for the present fiscal year, anyway. The present arrangements in connection with these adjournment proceedings are becoming increasingly unworkable.
I agree there is need for such a half hour period but I wonder whether there is need to provide as we do, for a seven minute question and a three minute answer. In most cases, half the time would be more than enough. I often feel that the questioner, or the responder, is trying to fill a much larger hole than the occasion calls for, simply to put in the time. We could process twice the number of questions and answers in the time now available and thus give these proceedings a reasonable chance of being timely.
Then, we have the old favourite, or new favourite, of Motion 43. The President of the Privy Council has already suggested we have covered a fair amount of territory with national emergencies which are raised on a daily basis. I certainly concur with one of his comments to the effect that there must be some better system for the carrying of these mini-debates, as he described them. I am not suggesting that this need be on a daily basis, but certainly an opportunity should be afforded to members from time to time to focus attention and response on issues which demand the attention of this institution.
I think I would agree with a comment which I believe the minister has made from time to time, but which was not part of his statement the other day. It is not quite fair for individual members to stand and present motions, sometimes at length, when there is no opportunity for a reply to be made. I think the President of the Privy Council has said that to be fair in this situation there must be some right of reply, limited as it should be, so that in dealing with the mini-debate a fair opportunity would be given to respond to the issue raised.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would now like to turn to one further area which I hope receives examination by the committee, that is, the whole area of standing committees. The President of the Privy Council made some remarks about the activities of the standing committees. There seems to be no doubt that the committee system will play an increasingly important role in the functions of this and future parliaments. But there are some very obvious shortcomings to our present committee system. I cannot possibly catalogue them all in the few minutes at my disposal here this afternoon, but let me briefly point to some of the more obvious aspects of the committee system which should be examined.
The size of the committees should be reviewed, to start with. We have, I understand, reduced the size of committees over the years as compared with the size of similar committees in the beginning. Only a few years ago, I 
understand, committees used to have memberships of up to 60. I do not know how they could ever have functioned in an effective manner and I rather doubt they did so. But I would argue that even committees made up of 25 or 20 members are still, in many instances, too large. My own experience in dealing with many committees, both of a political nature and of other kinds, is that once membership goes beyond 12, people are merely performing the function of being a body to be listed on the record. If these committees are to perform an active function, I think that something in the order of 12 members, and certainly not more than 15, is necessary to make up the permanent membership roll.
Another point I would make concerns membership itself. The President of the Privy Council rightly suggested that we have gone from one extreme with respect to membership to another. It used to be somewhat difficult, involving a time delay of one day, to change the membership on a committee as compared to the instant changes which can now be made. While I recognize there may be some necessity to retain an emergency procedure by which a full membership can be provided to a committee, the increasing frequency of changes which occurs in the membership of committees, a procedure which almost seems to be encouraged, is not good.
As anyone who has studied the committee system which exists in Washington will agree, there is a certain drawback in having a committee system which is so moribund that there can be no movement, as has happened under the well-known seniority system operating in the United States Congress. But I think we have gone to the other extreme, which is just as ridiculous, and has made the system almost meaningless. I believe that all members will wish to look very closely at the question of how we can upgrade the importance of the committees to the individual Member of Parliament, to the press and to the general public. We really cannot expect anybody else to take the committee system very seriously unless we do so ourselves. I do hope that this whole area will be given serious consideration.
There are, in my opinion, some straight physical problems we have not solved. It is ridiculous when you think, Mr. Speaker, that one of the problems we face when trying to arrange committee meetings is that of getting enough room. We do not have enough rooms available with translation and recording facilities to service the committees. In many instances we do not have enough staff. There is insufficient provision for the printing and distribution of reports. There is a whole host of just physical problems which should not be tolerated for one moment. If we are to operate in a contemporary and effective parliament we have to recognize that we need adequate committee rooms, committee staff and facilities to make the system work.
This ties in very closely with what was said by the President of the Privy Council about the scheduling of committees. We have made some improvements and experiments with regard to scheduling, but the cloak and dagger operation that we have now when scheduling committees is absolutely ludicrous. No modern parliament should put up with the kind of surprise and nonsense that
March 9, 1973

goes on in regard to when committees are or are not going to meet. We must have some established method whereby times of committee meetings are well known by all and are adhered to as much as possible.
I also relate this to the whole business of whether or not committees should be established on a permanent basis. It was questioned earlier in this debate whether we should have departmental reports along with estimates referred to committees, and whether this might well be made some kind of permanent arrangement so that, in effect, committees have a life that is ongoing.
There is another fundamental problem that I want to raise, and it is one of the reasons that I think the committee system is often turned into a cynical exercise by many Members of Parliament. I refer to the final product that often comes from a committee-its report and/or its recommendations. In this parliament, after a committee has laboured long and hard on a specific subject matter and makes a report to this House, there is clear cut machinery for the disposition of this report or its body of recommendations. During a brief conversation I had with a visiting British parliamentarian the other day, I was told that when his committee submits its report to parliament, the members of that committee know there will be a departmental or ministerial answer given within a recognized period of time. If committees are to become a serious element in our parliamentary processes, there has to be some kind of response to a report either from this institution itself, or from the minister or department to which the committee report relates.
I have spoken much longer than I should, Mr. Speaker, but I feel that this committee is an extremely important one and I hope it will do its job with great effectiveness for all members of this House.

speechtext:
It is my opinion that this discussion has been a poor one, which is almost an indication that this committee's work is doomed to failure before it starts. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) spoke at length. The House leader of the Conservative party spoke at length. My House leader-this was a rare exception in this particular case-did not speak at all; he was out making points in another place at the time. I think he made the right decision. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) also spoke, but from a different point of view.
Those who have participated in this debate have discussed the subject academically, it is the backbenchers who are really the members who should have made some input into this discussion. They have been here for a while now and should have said what they think is wrong with this place. Let us not have the mandarins of parliament
Standing Orders and Procedure
setting the rules and changing the rules. They have been shuffling the rules about for a long time now, and the last time they made changes to the rules the results were not satisfactory. What they did had the effect of eliminating the three back rows on both sides of this House. This is why I say the backbenchers should have made some input. They think they do not know anything about the rules, which is the only credible position to take in this House, and in my opinion it is the only credible input to the deliberations of the procedure committee.
Considerable reference has been made to the question period, but again I have the same criticism. The House leader, the opposition leader, the leader of my party and the leader of the Creditiste party set the question period. It is no longer a question period for members of parliament; let us not kid ourselves about that. We hire people to set the questions, and we are paying people to provide the answers to those questions. Again, the parties are making the decision as to who will ask the first question. We provide Mr. Speaker with a list of names of those who want to ask questions. John Blow from Dry Gulch wants to ask about a problem he has which is important to the people that he represents. Obviously, it is not a party matter or a matter of national importance, and he will not be able to ask his question unless he is provided with a totally different format for the question period.
I do not care if the question period is extended. The last speaker convinced me that it may be a good idea to have nothing in parliament except the question period. Perhaps this could be the microcosm for the representations that we make, and we would not handle any legislation at all. But I do not think that this is what the backbencher wants. He wants a way in which he can ask a stupid question, one that everybody else thinks is of no importance at all but which is of vital importance to the people whom he represents, and he sure ain't going to get into this question period that is now becoming as highly organized as any other segment of governmental operations.
I have been here for quite a while, Mr. Speaker, but I do not consider myself an expert on the procedures or on the rules of this House. I think the rules should remain as they are so I can use them, break them, or do with them whatever seems to suit my purpose at the time. If we keep changing the rules, it makes it more difficult for me. As I say, I think the new members of this House, particularly the young members, should have some input into this committee which they have not been allowed to have so far. We should not do what three or four previous speakers have said. We should not start with the idea that we must make this place function like a well-piled machine. We should start with the premise that every backbencher who has a problem in his area should be given the opportunity of doing something about it.
When I first came here the backbencher had that right if he had guts enough to exercise it. He was given that right in several ways, and one of the ways was to wait until the estimates came before the House. When we reached a certain item that related to the bridge that he wanted to see built over a particular river in his area, that was his chance. I can remember Mr. Van Horne, who represented Restigouche-Madawaska or some such riding, discussing such a matter over a period of time, and eventually a

March 9, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure bridge was built. I am not saying the bridge was built solely because he took advantage of that opportunity, but he did have the right to ask the officials questions about it. That right has now been taken away.
I think all hon. members should consider whether we should allow the parties to arrange the question period. I think Mr. Speaker has an obligation to the backbencher not to honour the list that is sent to him by the parties every day. I suggest that most Members of Parliament asking questions of particular interest to their ridings will not want to ask more than one supplementary question. The party microcosmic debate that takes place during the first and second questions usually relates to party matters rather than matters of concern to members.
For these reasons, I am sorry that more members do not take two or three minutes to outline the subjects they feel should be discussed by the procedural committee. They should get up and say what they think is wrong with this place, because obviously there is a lot wrong with it. There are too many who follow precedent and refer to authorities such as May and others. Most of us have never even bothered to open these books. They refer to precedents that are long gone. If the procedural committee looks at the Standing Orders and makes changes, I hope we can dispose of all the other books such as Beau-chesne's first edition, second edition, third edition, fourth edition as well as May's, Knowles and all the rest of them.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gillespie that Bill C-3, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-3 somewhat dismayed at its lack of scope. The bill, in effect, will increase the authorized capital of the Export Development Corporation from $7 million to $125 million and raise its allowable liability limit from $850 million to $1,500 million. What is lacking in my view is any mention of export assistance to small business. There is nothing whatever for our small, secondary industry in this piece of legislation.
The throne speech made mention of assistance to small business and here we have the first opportunity for the government to assist small business, yet nothing is forthcoming. I should have thought this bill would have made provision for a small businessmen's division. All over this country there are thousands of small industries making well designed products which could be exported, but they need help and guidance to enter this market. They should receive guidance, assistance and financial aid from the Export Development Corporation. We seem to spend considerable time in this House talking about wheat, fish, oil, Indians and even polar bears, and while I have every sympathy for these subjects and realize their importance, it seems to me far too little attention is paid to the labour intensive small business and secondary industry in Canada.
There is no shortage of talent or initiative in Canada. Only last evening I spoke by telephone with a member of my riding who started a new business in January manufacturing solid wooden toys. He asked me about a LIP grant of some $200,000 given to a motorcycle club in Montreal to assist it in manufacturing wooden toys. He asked me about the wisdom of the reduction in tariffs on toys featured in the budget speech of February 19. He
March 9. 1973

asked me to inform this government that all he really wants is a chance to have funds available to him at a reasonable rate of interest, allowing him to develop the full potential of his business. He also asked about export assistance.
That man is typical of the intelligent and aggressive Canadian businessman who must somehow get the attention of all governments to make them realize how vital the contribution of these businessmen is to our economy, and what a great contribution they could make in lowering the level of unemployment on a permanent basis. We have such promise and so much potential it is frustrating to those of us who see the picture clearly. There is such an abundance of raw material, a talented and intelligent population with industrial skills, business and secondary educational facilities to feed these industrial skills, and we know we need only put them all together to make things work.
So long as we continue to introduce into this House bills such as C-3, which completely ignores the small businesses and secondary industries of Canada, we will continue to flounder and flop with the grievous level of unemployment we have today. I think it is time we looked at that very seriously. A few weeks ago the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) introduced a private members' motion to raise the limit on loans under the Small Business Loans Act from $25,000 to $75,000. I spoke in support of that motion. The hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson), I am sure on instructions, talked out the motion. In reviewing that action, and on reading the contents of Bill C-3, I can only conclude that although this government gives lip service to the cause of small business it is in effect antismall business.
I have travelled in approximately 35 different countries of the world. I have observed how other countries assist businesses. I have travelled over most of Europe and somewhat in Asia. In northern Sweden, I visited a town about 40 miles south of the Arctic Circle where there is an exhibition centre devoted exclusively to products manufactures in northern Sweden. Trade missions from all over the world visit this exhibition centre and orders are taken on the spot. All arrangements are made there. All export details are available at the exhibition centre. Their banks will advance funds to a manufacturer or processor against an export order. In other words, they are tuned to an export market as well as a domestic market.
In Great Britain, the merchant banking system is tuned to export business. A small businessman, whether a processor or manufacturer, has a relatively easy task compared to a Canadian small businessman. He prepares his export documents and has his money within 48 hours of presentation of shipping documents. The small businessman works closely with the merchant banking system in that country. I believe it is significant that our party leader has recommended this system or one similar to it for Canada. I hope we have the opportunity to introduce such a system in the not too distant future. German banks now deal directly on short-term paper with Canadian customers at pretty low rates of interest compared to what we have in this country at the present time.
Export Development Act
There seems to be a reluctance on the part of the government to take a stand on secondary industry and the [DOT] role of the small business in Canadian economic life. The Gibson Report of May 14, 1968 reads in part:
Giving exports a high priority does not take away from other desirable national objectives such as better housing or regional development. On the contrary the well-based industrial growth to which export-oriented policies would contribute is the essential element of the higher production on which advances on welfare must be based. Giving exports a high priority is essential if reasonable progress is to be made in other directions.
"Reasonable progress in other directions" were the last words in that quotation. If we are to make reasonable progress in the reduction of unemployment in this country, the government must take a firm stand on the part secondary industry and small business will play in our national economy. A sound export directive must be part of that stand and a strong aggressive policy for secondary industry and small business must be the key ingredient of that policy.
In my view the government must stop the practice of playing off the production of our secondary industry against export sales of unfinished and semi-finished raw materials when settling our balance of payments accounts. We will never establish a strong secondary industry position while this policy persists. The government, I believe, must also stop the practice of bartering away the tariff protection of our secondary industry at GATT conferences. Mr. Benson's move to accelerate the Kennedy Round tariff cuts turned out to be a major setback for secondary industry in Canada. We might look at Japan and Germany where there is zero unemployment. Both these countries have tariffs protecting their industries. We seem to be the leader in promoting absolute free trade at the expense of our small business and secondary industry.
I would have thought that Bill C-3 would have announced the establishment of regional offices for the Export Development Corporation in the five major regions of Canada. Small business and secondary industry has always been the whipping boy of Liberal governments. Mr. Benson reduced tariffs at an accelerated rate to control inflation, he said. He meant: "Get back in line boys; we will bring in outside competition and if you don't want to bring down your own prices we will show you how to do it". Canada is the only signatory to the GATT agreement who slavishly abides by all the rules. I do not advocate wholesale breaking of the rules, but we do see other countries bend the rules to suit their national purpose while we hold fast to the agreement. Other countries with whom we trade impose surcharges, set up special legislation such as DISC, or raise tariffs against our manufactured goods while at the same time seeking dutyfree status for their exports to Canada. I think that until we put all these pieces together we will not make very much progress. We have in this country, I believe, an abundance of talented people, creative, ingenious people crying out to express their talents as entrepreneurs. They are stalled at every turn of the road.
In my riding I have an aggressive, talented small manufacturer who has designed, and is marketing, a unique product. He exports almost all his production. He is frustrated by his inability to obtain adequate financing in

March 9, 1973
Export Development Act
Canada. He is considering moving his office to New York State. He was approached by a United States group and asked to move into a plant they will build for him. A new company would be formed and he would have 49 per cent of the stock. They suggested to him that they would set up a DISC operation and export back into Canada. I think this is a critical situation. We really must get together and talk to the small business people and the people in the secondary industries of this country in an effort to develop policies which would aid them in their efforts to move ahead.
Mr. Speaker, 90 per cent of the small businesses in this country are Canadian owned. We need strong policies to encourage growth in this area of our economy. An export policy tuned to small business and secondary industry is a cornerstone to the growth we must have in this area. Any thinking businessman will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the only way we will beat unemployment in this country is by encouraging our small businesses and secondary industry. It is the responsibility of the government to create an economic climate in which business, particularly small business, can grow and prosper. The essential elements in that climate are: banking facilities that will supply the financial needs of business and encourage them to venture and expand their facilities; a tax act that they can understand and work within; a competition act based on reality and devoid of the hollow protected idealism of that infamous instrument introduced in the 28th Parliament; consumer legislation that is fair and just to the consumer and the producer or manufacturer. We need tariff legislation that is realistic in today's market and tuned to the needs of our secondary industry; we need an export policy that makes provision for the needs and requirements of small business and secondary industry and that would serve as well the large established manufacturers who, of course, must be part of the package that we put together for business.
These six essential elements must be the cornerstone of any national industrial strategy, if there is such a thing. We hear it talked about. I have not heard it defined very well, but these are the things we need to make business go and to allow it to grow in this country. I am a businessman myself and I have gone through all the frustrations of tight money, through the experience of planning an operation for a long period of time, of acquiring property and of hoping to build, only to have my plan turned down by the bank. We cannot continue to develop with policies such as these.
If this bill passes second reading, let me, through you, Mr. Speaker, serve notice on the minister that we will make strong representations at the committee level to have this legislation amended. There is a feeling among some people that there is some urgency in the passage of this bill. It has been suggested that perhaps the Export Development Corporation has exceeded its allowable limits, and of course by passing this legislation we can legalize an illegality. Be that as it may, I do not think that should cause us to rush through our consideration of the bill because, as I said at the beginning, this is the first opportunity the government has to do something for small and medium sized businesses. I say that, regardless of

what else goes on, we should stop here, take a long look at this bill and do what we can.
