speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the remarks of the hon. gentleman who just concluded his speech. I must say that some of the proposals put forward in general terms by some of the Conservative members for the reform of the Export Development Corporation in order to make it more helpful to small manufacturers and businesses in this country have a considerable amount of merit. I hope the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) will take a serious look at that aspect of the corporation's work. The Export Development Corporation plays an important role in a country such as ours which is so dependent upon export trade.
If I look at the table on page 20 of the report of the Export Development Corporation for 1971, I see an analysis of commodities insured in 1971 for export. I note that 32 per cent of the principal commodities insured were wood and other products related thereto and 23 per cent were agricultural products, which are of some significance to those of us in the west. Livestock, for example, was insured through the Export Development Corporation for a little over $2.5 million, and the shipment of wheat was insured for around $82 million. So, there is some merit in the activity of the Export Development Corporation. But a corporation which works in such close alliance with the large multinational corporations in our country is open to considerable criticism as well.
At page 6 of the annual report, you will see a breakdown of credit insurance policies as carried out by the corporation, and on looking at that breakdown you will see the types of goods that have been insured by the corporation. One area that interests me above all others is investment abroad. According to those who espouse the outdated free enterprise system, whether they come from my right or across the way, when you make an investment, either abroad or at home, you are supposed to be
March 9, 1973

taking a risk-at least that is what I have always assumed. In fact, some of my good friends close to my right often say that I have never taken a risk in terms of going into business. But I think this is one part of the Export Development Corporation which needs very serious examination.
It is a fact that the corporation is now moving into the area of insuring Canadian investment abroad. What this means is that $14 million of investment by Canadians is being insured by our government for investment mainly in the area of the Caribbean and Central America. We in this nation have often looked with a great deal of hesitation at the foreign control of our economy through investment by the United States and Great Britain. Now, however, we have established an Export Development Corporation, which in principle is of merit in terms of assisting certain nations to buy our commodities and to increase our exports, but which now moves into the area of insuring investment in foreign countries. To my mind that is eliminating the risk from investments, and I think the corporation should cease to involve itself in foreign investments of this nature. I find that 39 per cent of the inquiries concerning foreign investment relate to investment in the area of the Caribbean and Central America.
We have operated in conjunction with what is called the Inter-American Development Bank and we have been involved in it to the tune of $100 million for development in Central America. I do not think we should involve ourselves in backing private investors who are seeking, in some sense of the word, to exploit the areas of Central America and the Caribbean. We do not have to involve ourselves through a public operation in backing those investors. I suggest that if they wish to invest in those areas they should take the risk of investment. I think this is important.
Then, there is another area within the annual report relating to what I would call invisible exports. These cover such things as the sale and licencing to foreign customers of any right in a Canadian patent, trademark or copyright.
In that regard I think there should be serious examination of whether it is in Canada's interest for a public corporation to be backing such things as the sale or licensing to a foreign customer of any patent or copyright. I believe it is potentially dangerous for a public corporation to promote any such open trade on behalf of the Canadian public.
On page 7 of the annual report of the corporation it is stated:
EDC has, in co-operation with Statistics Canada, nearly completed a survey of the 'terms of credit' granted by some 1,100 major Canadian exporters. When the results of this survey have been studied, it is hoped that the information collected can be interpreted and translated by EDC to determine to what extent EDC is meeting the requirements of Canadian exporters.
Considering the fact that Statistics Canada has grown so much during recent years, it is good to see a reference in one annual report to the fact that it is doing some work. But we should not be dealing with this bill or giving serious consideration to amendments to improve it, such as suggested by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth 25789-59*
Export Development Act
(Mr. Kempling) in his excellent speech, until we see that report. I hope it will come before the committee when we are discussing this legislation there. I trust the minister is listening closely to this point.
The report details certain financing agreements with foreign countries. One is Australia, and the transaction involved railway hopper cars. As one who comes from the prairie region, this is a subject that interests me greatly. The amount of the financing was $10,355,916. It was for the purchase of railway hopper cars, the exporter being the National Steel Car Corporation Limited. It would be interesting to have a comparison of the price at which Australians bought these hopper cars with the price which our government paid for 2,000 hoppers cars for the railways in Canada, which was over $40 million. This is a matter we should seriously examine in committee.
There are many other items I could mention but I will not go into them all today. The Export Development Corporation shows us that to a certain extent a public corporation can be involved in promoting the export of Canadian goods and that the government can play a role. We can give our tacit approval to that. But there is a problem. That problem concerns whether the corporation is acting in the public interest when all it does primarily is promote exports by foreign-owned, multinational corporations.
The corporation is serving multinational corporations at the expense of smaller, independent businesses in Canada. It is giving multinational corporations an advantage in addition to those they already enjoy in terms of write-offs by the U.S. government, the DISC program and many other breaks that they receive. Now those corporations can play off the government of Canada against other governments, at the expense of smaller, independent operators in this country.
When I talk philosophically about the relationship between government and business, there immediately comes to mind the program called Interchange Canada. I wonder how far this is a sweetheart relationship between multinational corporations, large Canadian corporations and the government of Canada. Is it in the interest of the ordinary people of this country? For example, through Interchange Canada the president of Labatt's Ontario Breweries Limited takes a job with the Department of Industry and Commerce, and in exchange a senior civil servant will work for a large, multinational corporation in order to gain experience in the private business sector. This develops a sort of sweetheart relationship between the two groups.
The president of Labatt's will be running a foreign exchange, export program. He was recently quoted as comparing the role of the civil servant with the role of the businessman. He says the similarities are fairly easy to identify. The taxpayer would seem to occupy the same place in a public servant's mind as does the shareholder in the mind of the business executive. That was not good news to me, Mr. Speaker. It means that shareholders and taxpayers are both irrelevant so far as the upper echelons of the civil service and of the corporate elite are concerned. He also said that parliament, or more particularly the cabinet, can be compared to the board of directors of a private firm. That is not good news to me, either. This kind of sweetheart relationship evidenced in some aspects

March 9, 1973
Export Development Act
of the Export Development Corporation and the Interchange Canada program can be potentially detrimental to the public interest. It is not an open kind of relationship.
I am sure I could go back to my area and find a dozen producers who would like nothing better than to be able to operate the Department of Agriculture for a couple of weeks. They could probably straighten it out better than some of the economists who have been in it for 30 years. I tie these things together to underline my initial valid criticisms.
I believe that the government's moving in the area of insuring foreign investment and taking the element of risk right out proves there should be more involvement of public investment within this country simply because there is no real risk. By assisting investment in other countries the government is helping them to become imperialistic, a problem which we face in our own country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this debate on second reading of Bill C-3. I hope the debate will conclude today so that we can send this important bill to committee and have a detailed examination of the activities of the Export Development Corporation, its approaches and philosophies. In his speech on second reading, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) welcomed this opportunity.
Mr. Speaker, the Export Development Corporation is a successful part of this government. Its scope has been improved by us. We are proud of it and we welcome the opportunity to tell the public how good the EDC has been to the Canadian economy. It has provided jobs for Canadians by financing Canadian suppliers abroad and by making loans to foreign buyers of Canadian products.
Members of the opposition, especially in the Conservative party, have raised the question of the activities of the EDC, claiming that they are not oriented enough toward small business. Of course, this is a reflection of the narrow point of view that the Conservative party attaches to any discussion of this sort by trying to confuse the facts. They are attempting to say that because the EDC is involved in major loans to major suppliers, and because it looks after large projects, it does not do anything at all for small business.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: I did not say anything about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) does not have to be concerned about this, because I mentioned the Conservative party and not the whole opposition, although I know that sometimes his party does not make any more sense than the Conservative party. I am speaking of the Conservative criticism of EDC in claiming that it supports only large suppliers. This is not the case, Mr. Speaker. Anybody knows that, by nature, assistance to foreign buyers or suppliers will be given to large companies. But we must not forget the spin-off across the country. For instance, a loan of $10 million to a foreign buyer to enable him to place an order with Northern Electric would result in orders for a multiplicity of small businesses across the country and as many as 4,000 sup-

pliers might be involved. Even if the loan is arranged so that Northern Electric is the supplier, it does not mean that it is the only company to benefit, because the components required to fill the order might be manufactured by various suppliers who are mainly small businessmen.
An assembly order placed with the Montreal locomotive works would result in only 20 per cent being spent with them; the remaining 80 per cent would be spread among small suppliers across the country. Because EDC is mainly involved with large transactions we should not conclude that they are not interested in small suppliers. Despite the positive effect that it has on small businesses through the larger transactions, there are other programs that affect small business directly, such as the export credits insurance program. This has about 1,000 policyholders, 700 of whom have less than $250,000 worth of exports per year: they can hardly be categorized as large companies. That is one program that helps many small businessmen across the country.
The Conservatives and members of the other opposition parties omitted to mention the re-lending program of the EDC which is available through Canadian banks in foreign countries and which, upon reference by EDC, arranges for assistance to be given to small suppliers.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: What volume?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Just a moment. Re-lending is available to foreign banks or foreign correspondents of Canadian banks, and they are authorized to lend as little as $50,000 to buyers of capital equipment or services in Canada from small Canadian manufacturers. When a state agency or buyer in another country is talking about a transaction with Canadian businessmen and it involves special financing, that automatically is a large order. Therefore it is normal that most transactions of the EDC are large.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

This government has given incentives to Canadian businessmen. It has done that for many years with many programs involving the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and all sorts of lending programs. Those programs are good for Canadian business. The opposition is trying to throw up a smokescreen on this issue by saying, we should deal with the foreign-ownership problem only by giving incentives to Canadian businessmen. Of course we want to give them incentives, but incentives alone will not deal with the question of foreign ownership. The best description of the Tory policy on foreign ownership was that given by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce when he called it a nonpolicy; it was superficial nonsense. That describes adequately Tory policy on foreign ownership.

That is what the hon.
Export Development Act
member would do, but that would not deal with the foreign ownership problem at all.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

There could be a problem regarding foreign ownership in this country, but we will discuss that at the appropriate time. Let us discuss it in the proper context and let us not, in the meantime, introduce all sorts of confusion and distort facts by saying that the Export Development Corporation is not doing its job, or that the job it is doing is terrible because it lends money to foreign corporations.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: When did we say that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
If our manufacturing industry is controlled too much by foreign interests, we will deal with that question when the time comes. Surely we cannot deal with this problem by discriminating against foreign companies. In other words, surely we should not try to hamper the export of Canadian products merely because the Conservatives have no policy on foreign investment.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe tried to confuse the issue by raising the question of domestic needs. He mentioned urban transportation. I had to re-read his speech because at first I could not believe it. He spoke about the Export Development Corporation lending so much money at such and such interest rates. That was the speech of a man who has experience with the financial institutions of this country. Apparently he does not understand that there is a world of difference between lending rates domestically and lending rates internationally.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: There sure is a difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Of course there is. This situation is not confined to Canada alone; it is an international condition. Canadian exporters, whether foreign or domestically owned, must compete, not only with lending institutions of other countries which offer services to potential buyers of our products all over the world, and sometimes offer better rates and concessional financing, but with the financial organizations and institutions of other governments which specialize in export financing. Examples of these are to be found in the United States, Europe and Japan.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe was upset because of the difference between the interest rates the EDC charges exporters and the rates that are available to Canadian businessmen. Canadian businessmen in the domestic market do not have to export and meet competitive rates on the international market.

speechtext:
Yes, they should vote against it if they do not want the Canadian government to help Canadian suppliers who sell abroad. If that is what the Conservatives want the Canadian government to help Canadian suppliers who sell abroad. If that is what the Conservatives
The hon. member is trying to make people believe that the government is subsidizing these low rates. Nothing is further from the truth. One must consider this question in the context of costs and benefits. In some cases, depending on the rates which the corporation has to pay for its money from the government, there could be a loss. As I say, it could happen that the corporation could lose money on some agreements in order to meet competition from other countries. When that happens, the loss is borne by the EDC and not by the government.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: And who owns the EDC?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
One can look at the financial statements. The EDC accounts for its operations every year. If hon. members find that the EDC is operating at a loss, we could discuss in this House the question of whether we should pay that loss or not. Sometimes the corporation must lose money in order to meet competition. I emphasize this point: it must meet competition. It could be that a Canadian supplier who wants to sell his product in Turkey will compete with a Japanese supplier who has access to better rates of interest, or the Japanese supplier might offer the buyer better rates of interest. In that case it is up to the EDC to accommodate the Canadian supplier, because it is important for the Canadian firm to make the sale.
The cost of money from the treasury, as all hon. members know, can and does vary from time to time. It depends on the average cost of government borrowings. If it has cost the government 6 per cent to borrow money, the treasury's lending rate to the EDC would be 6-1/8 per cent. These rates vary every three months. From time to time EDC's borrowing costs are high because the government's borrowing costs are high, and losses occur when the EDC is forced to give guarantees at lower rates. It could be that the original arrangement was made when money from the government was available only at high rates. If there is loss, that loss must be borne by the EDC.
Currently, the average cost of money for the EDC to meet outstanding loans is 5-7/8 per cent, whereas the average yields on these loans is about 7-1/8 per cent. This means that there is a margin of about 1-1 per cent. That is hardly operating at a loss, no matter how the accounting is done in the banks. Even if the EDC at times has to sustain a loss, it is totally contrary to the facts for hon. members to say that the low interest rates charged by the EDC are subsidized by the government. The hon. member for York-Simcoe tried to argue that the government should subsidize domestic interest rates, or in some way
make available better rates for domestic needs. Priorities have to be decided in connection with spending on domestic needs. At this point discussions are going on between the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the provinces on the subject of urban transportation. To try to compare these two factors is not fair at all.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has expressed concern lately that the ceiling under which the EDC operates has been exceeded; that the loans outstanding amount to more than the ceiling allowed. I realize he is a new member of this House and that he may not be aware of the terms of the legislation, but I would invite him to read section 30 of the act. If after doing so he is still confused, I would be glad to spend five minutes showing him how it works.

Did you read your own financial
statement?

speechtext: The hon. member who is interrupting is new to this House and I would hardly expect that he has read section 30 of the act. As I say, I would be happy to take five minutes explaining it to hon. members opposite. It might be, though, that they would still be confused.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: You don't understand it yourself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
I do. Maybe the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has not read section 30, either. It has been alleged that because the EDC has to date signed financing agreements totalling $865 million, it has already exceeded its existing statutory lending ceiling under section 30 of the act. This is not the position. The confusion arises because of a misunderstanding as to what is meant by the ceiling. Under section 30, the corporation may not have instruments outstanding at any time in excess of $850 million. As of January 31, 1973, the level of instruments outstanding totalled $500 million.
Instruments become outstanding only when disbursements are made under signed financing agreements. Disbursements take place over an extended period after the signing of financial agreements. Concurrently during this period instruments are being retired as repayments of principal are made on loans outstanding. The corporation may therefore sign financing agreements somewhat in excess of the ceiling applicable to instruments as long as this never obliges the EDC to purchase instruments exceeding the statutory ceiling. And it has not done so. Maybe the hon. member has not read the act carefully. Maybe he thought the ceiling applied to financial agreements.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: And I still do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext: That is not the case.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on Bill C-3 and try to get a few answers from someone on the government side in explanation of its purpose. I thought the parliamentary secretary might have given us some answers. It is Friday afternoon. I want to leave early today and I do not want to go home with my stomach and mind all upset.
After listening to the ranting and raving of the parliamentary secretary, I am beginning to wonder why he got to his feet at all. He gave us no reason for asking for this increase in the ceiling. He did make a number of vague accusations against member: on this side, alleging some of them had said the corporation ought to be wiped out, that it was no good. I defy the hon. member to show that anyone on this side has ever questioned the validity of the corporation's role. What we have said, and what I want to repeat, is this: while the corporation is worthy of support in principle, we question the way in which its funds have been administered.
We also question the tactics of the government of overspending and trying to do indirectly, by warrant, what it cannot do directly. We have seen examples of this before now. The latest concerned the Unemployment Insurance
Export Development Act
Commission. The funds were overspent and the government had to come back to parliament to get the ceiling removed. In that case there was some excuse because as a result of the government's policies and government bungling, unemployment insurance benefits cost a billion dollars more than was estimated; the money had to be spent and it had to be replaced.
Surely, though, there can be no excuse for bringing in this bill demanding another half a billion dollars to be made available to exporters. They will not tell us how much they have put out to date, or how much they are committed to advancing in the next few months. My hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has been trying to get this information, and his words have been construed by the parliamentary secretary as a condemnation of the corporation. The parliamentary secretary had better read our speeches again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he goes on to another point? He referred to special warrants. Is he implying that the Export Development Corporation has benefited in some way from Governor General's warrants?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: The hon. member had better sit there and listen for a while. He cannot understand what people are saying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Do you know what you are saying?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
We are not denying the value of the principle here. I agree that exports are a vital part of the Canadian economy and it is essential we should develop exports in order to create jobs and keep the economy moving. I realize that over the past few years exports have shown a steady increase and that the prospects this year are excellent. But I question whether much of this development can be attributed directly to the activities of the Export Development Corporation.
To establish the basis for my remarks, which are an endeavour to get some answers and the reasons behind this request for an increase of half a billion dollars, let me say something about the rationale for the Export Development Corporation, about the reason that was given in 1969 for the formation of the corporation. At that time the minister who introduced the bill, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who at that time was speaking for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, said as recorded at page 7474 of Hansard:
-exports are an essential key to our industrial development policies, providing as they do outlets beyond our limited domestic market.
I will not quote the minister verbatim, but in the next paragraph he goes on to say this:
In the interest, then, of optimum growth of the economy and of employment opportunities, stimulation of exports, particularly of manufactured goods, should have high priority at this stage of our economic development.
The minister went on to say that the purpose of the act is to make it easier for exporters to finance their sales. That being the case, my interpretation of the primary purpose of the Export Development Corporation is the

March 9, 1973
Export Development Act
creation of jobs by increasing exports. Therefore, when the minister comes to this House asking for another half a billion dollars, I think we should ask him some questions about his request. Many questions have been put to him, but one question I should like him to answer, either here or in the committee, is what figures can he produce to indicate the number of jobs that have been created by loans granted to the EDC?
Before the minister rises to his feet, let me inform him I have looked through the annual report of the EDC and through other material in which I thought I might find these figures, but the only information I have obtained so far in this regard has been from the minister's speech of February 2 when he was talking about outstanding loans amounting to $700 million which had the equivalent value in jobs of roughly 100,000. I should like to know where he gets this figure. Is it a figure that he has just pulled out of the air? Does the minister mean that this $700 million has created 100,000 new jobs, or does he mean that if we had not financed these companies to the tune of $700 million, these 100,000 jobs would vanish? I have not been able to find the answer to that question, so I hope the minister will give us the basis for the figures when he replies.
The only explanation I have seen of this request to increase the ceiling by an extra half a billion dollars is the minister's statement that the corporation needs more money. The hon. member for York-Simcoe and others have tried time and again to get from the minister some accurate figures of the actual amount of money that has been expended or is left. The minister keeps telling us that the $850 million has not been used up. However, it is interesting to note that in reply to question No. 903 on February 28-a written reply to the question put down by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer)-the minister said that the total dollar amount of signed contracts under section 29 of the Export Development Act, as of December 31, 1972, was $841 million.
That was as at the end of December, and since then the figures I have been able to find indicate roughly $60 million more has been committed. That information I derived from news releases, and so on, put out by the Export Development Corporation. Between $6 million and $9 million has come back in the form of interest. This indicates to me that the total amount outstanding by way of commitments must be about $900 million, if the minister's figures are correct.
The parliamentary secretary went into quite a tirade, accusing members on this side of not being able to read or able to understand the act. He referred to section 30 of the Export Development Act. As I understood what he said, he implied that the ceiling does not matter until the funds are actually disbursed: in other words, you can go ahead and commit $1 billion or even twice that; the actual ceiling applies only when the funds are disbursed.
Another question that I do not think will be answered by the parliamentary secretary, but which I should like to put to the minister, is this. On page 18 of the 1971 annual report published by the Export Development Corporation, under the heading "Notes to Financial Statements" there is a statement that does not agree with what the parliamentary secretary was trying to tell the House. I will read it:
The authority to guarantee and lend on the security of instruments under sections 29 and 30 of the Export Development Act is limited to $850 million outstanding at any one time.
What does "outstanding" mean? The note goes on to say:
As at December 31, 1971, the corporation had undertaken undisbursed authorizations aggregating $262,539,000. The uncommitted authority to guarantee and lend on the security of instruments as at December 31, 1971, amounted to $212,769,000. The aggregate of outstanding notes receivable as at December 31, 1971, under section 29 amounted to $374,692,000.
If you total those three amounts, Mr. Speaker, you have exactly $850 million, so my interpretation of that section is that not only disbursed amounts but also committed amounts are to be considered under the ceiling of $850 million. Perhaps the minister would explain that point in his remarks here or in the committee.
I go back to my initial point, that what we are concerned with here is not so much an analysis of the EDC and its functions. Of course the corporation has made mistakes, every corporation has. But I want to know whether Canadians have received full value for their money. When putting forward the rationale for setting up this corporation, the minister made it quite clear that the primary purpose of these funds was the creation of employment. My question to the minister is this: Is he satisfied that this $850 million or $1 billion that is being granted in foreign loans is doing the job it is intended to do? Could we not have created more jobs, or as many jobs by assisting industries in Canada to sell in Canada?
To emphasize what I am saying, let me refer once again to the remarks of the hon. member for Trinity when speaking to this matter in the House on February 2. At that time he pointed out very clearly that while it is fine to export, there is a quid pro quo; something has to come back. The old philosophy that a country can survive by exporting alone probably goes back to the days when England ruled the waves. But the fact is that a healthy economy today depends on the total aggregate of demand, not only for exports but for what is produced for domestic consumption.
I suggest that if this $1 billion was spent in Canada to assist Canadian manufacturing to meet domestic demands, it would create more than 100,000 jobs, the figure that the minister tossed around so cavalierly. This is our point; it is not a condemnation of the EDC as such.
These are some of the things the minister has to answer in committee. How much has he committed over the next two or three years? What value did he get for this money? How many jobs has he created? Does he think it is fair to send money to foreign customers when we have provinces, municipalities and other government bodies crying for more funds but receiving the stock answer that this government cannot provide more housing or money for transportation because the economy cannot stand it? These are the questions I want answered when this bill is considered by the committee. In conclusion I say that we are anxious to get the bill to the committee where we can perhaps get some straight answers from the minister. If the minister can satisfy us that we are getting full value

March 9, 1973

for our dollars then, as far as I am concerned, we should let the bill pass third reading.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: My remarks will be somewhat brief, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Good.

speechtext:
That seems to please the hon. member for Hull, but to get to Bill C-3 which is before us, I observe that the aim is to increase the corporation's shares and at the same time enable it also to increase its loan possibilities.
Before introducing a bill such as Bill C-3, the government should perhaps review the use of funds invested in the corporation.
In the past, has the Export Development Corporation served the interests of Canadian manufacturers, or has it merely put its funds to use by large multinational corporations? These are questions that we should ask ourselves.
Under the terms of this bill, we would be accepting that the corporation be obliged to restrict its aid to basically Canadian companies. Since they are talking about industrial controls, I should have thought that this would be just the indirect way of favouring our Canadian industries and manufacturers.
Mr. Speaker, increasing share capital and raising the ceiling for loans seems quite appropriate to me, especially considering the spiraling costs in all areas. I therefore feel that the government's request is logical.
We cannot therefore criticize the increase as such, but we can be most sceptical about the allotment of funds. We feel that it is necessary to assist exportation, even to promote it, but this bill and some others in no way guarantee that the Canadian people will be served first, before our products are sold abroad.
What protection does the government give to the Canadian consumer? The party in power seems to believe that we can resort to any means to export our production. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Breau) said a while ago that the corporation even granted loans to other countries to purchase our production.
In my opinion, if the government is in position to increase the assets and shares of the corporation, it should in the first place increase the purchasing power of the Canadian people who in many cases are deprived of the products whose exportation is now promoted by the government.
As always, this government reshuffles the order of priority of his motions and again, we see it favouring foreigners to the detriment of Canadians or, to be more accurate, coming to the aid of foreigners before taking care of the basic needs of Canadians.
I may be repeating myself but why should we not introduce a bill to restrict exports until we have satisfied the essential needs of Canadians? Then the government could draft a bill designed to protect Canadian producers through preferential export loans, granted only to Canadian firms and only for export of our surpluses. Should
Export Development Act
need arise to stimulate the export of these surpluses, the government could introduce a bill such as the one before us today and thus favour export as such. But again, I repeat, only as a last resort.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the gist of my remarks. I am not criticising the government for its intention to increase the potential of the corporation, but I regret that it did not deem necessary to respect the needs of Canadians and then guarantee protection of essentially Canadian companies before merely promoting exports.

I should like to say a few words before four o'clock, Mr. Speaker, on one or two grave concerns which I have about Bill C-3. On the surface it looks rather innocent. It will increase the capital shares of the corporation to $125 million and increase loan guarantees from $800 million to $1,500 million. There are two areas of grave concern. The first is that the corporation tends to be big business or multinational corporation oriented. Perhaps the experience members of the Liberal party have had with multinational corporations tends to prejudice them in that direction. At any rate, this is one of my concerns.
All one has to do is pick up the annual report of the corporation and look at the first, second and third pages to see who is on the board of directors. We find there is an interrelationship between the government and big business or multinational corporations. It might be of interest to the House if I named some of the directors. First of all we have James Grandy, who is the deputy-minister of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He is chairman of the board. We have other government mandarins, such as L. C. Audette, who is chairman of the Tariff Board, Paul Gerin-Lajoie, who is president of CIDA, and S. S. Reisman, deputy-minister of the Department of Finance. We also have Louis Rasminsky, the former governor of the Bank of Canada.
Let us look at the corporate side. Serving as the corporation's president we have Paul Leman, president of the Aluminum Company of Canada; we have A. F. Mayne, president of A. F. Mayne & Associates Limited, Montreal; we have R. D. Southern, president of Atco Industries Limited, Calgary; and we have P. R. Sandwell, who is chairman of the board of Sandwell & Company Limited, Vancouver. All these people are presidents of various corporations, so obviously there is a tremendous relationship between government mandarins and the presidents of corporations in respect of the activities of the Export Development Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it four o'clock and pursue some of these ideas further at a later date?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, to provide for the establishment of the Alaska-Yukon Highway Authority (Alaska Highway), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the matter I have the pleasure to introduce to this House this afternoon is neither an ordinary bill nor an ordinary subject matter. It is a Canadian legend, a Canadian shrine-the matter of the Alaska Highway.
This year the Department of Public Works has a very ambitious maintenance and construction program in respect of the Alaska Highway. In addition to normal maintenance work, tenders have been called for two gravel resurfacing maintenance projects from mile 250 to mile 413, from mile 413 to mile 483 and reconstruction of another section. This work is scheduled for completion by the fall of 1973. There are other minor innovations to the highway plan for this year.
Hon. members probably assume that I will speak about the highway with the idea of having it completed, of having further work done and eventually having it built so that it will be a transportation link between the United States and that province of the north called Alaska. However, I would like to speak about some of the other aspects in connection with this Canadian dream, or legend.
The construction of the Alaska Highway had been proposed for many years before the outbreak of World War II. However, it was not until the Japanese occupied some of the Aleutian Islands and threatened the air ferry supply to Russia that a highway was actively considered. Construction of a pioneer road by engineer troops followed rapidly on the heels of the location crews. Speed was the first consideration and this road detoured around swamps, gullies, rock knolls and other obstructions, resulting in a very crooked road with many steep grades.
After August, 1942, efforts were directed to getting the pioneer trail converted to a passable road at the earliest possible moment. This road disregarded the public roads administration procedures, where design alignment and grade would delay completion, and followed the path of least resistance. In March, 1943, instructions were issued to complete the work at the minimum possible cost and standards were reduced still further. Road construction ceased in October, 1943, but bridge construction continued until 1944.
The resulting highway, while passable and providing a good gravel driving surface, had geometries of a varying but generally poor standard. After the responsibility of the highway was transferred from the United States army to the Royal Canadian Engineers, the terms of reference under which they operated did not permit major road relocations. Temporary bridges were replaced by perma-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
nent structures at many locations and some exceptionally hazardous areas were reconstructed, but the alignment of the highway is essentially that of 1943. In 1959-1961, the highway was paved to RAU 50 standard from mile 0 to 84. This standard provided two 12-foot traffic lanes and 5-foot shoulders. The British Columbia department of highways has been responsible for the maintenance of the paved section since 1962.
After this brief outline of history of this great highway linking our northern regions to the more developed area of our country, I would like the members of this House, whose support I am asking, to recognize the important part played in the past by the Alaska Highway and the much more important part that it will play in the future development of our last frontier. Many tales are told of pioneers, past and present, travelling this road and many chapters of history have been written about the legends of this highway. I am more concerned about the implications of the highway and its benefits in recent times.
First we must consider the economic state of affairs in the Peace River country and in the northern part of British Columbia, where farming has suffered a severe setback. The farming situation is disastrous. The copper mines have closed. The economy of Fort Nelson is in a disastrous state. The government so far has disregarded the plight of that area in respect of all its programs such as DREE.
In 1966, the Stanford report was prepared for the government. It recommended that any further action in respect of the highway be shelved for at least ten years and that the government should not be concerned about the development of our northland and the development of our resources since the highway is an outdated mode of transportation for the movement of goods and people today, when we have jet airplanes and other more up to date modes of transportation. I am not in conflict, of course, with that statement in the report if one considers only the need to find, extract and exploit our natural resources and does not consider the human factor, the people who live there, our first citizens and early settlers, and does not consider that even in that region, with all the modern facilities of transportation, people would be required in order to develop and populate the area.
I am also concerned about the industries already located in northern British Columbia and the Yukon territory, as well as the plight of these industries through not having a proper means of transportation for the shipment of their products and for the maintenance of the work force in their plants. All the resources of the great region of the Yukon must be shipped, or are presently being shipped by an outmoded transportation system to a port linked to Alaska and end up in ports strange to our land. I am very excited about the plans announced for the northern part of British Columbia in respect of the transportation network, and I am hopeful that the government will seriously consider helping industries locate in northern British Columbia and the Yukon territory by the provision of proper transportation facilities.
I am encouraged by the plans of the British Columbia railways. The line has now been extended to Fort Nelson, 300 miles up the highway. An ambitious program to extend the line even further is being planned. The empha-
March 9, 1973

sis on northern development in that region must not be concentrated around the extraction of our resources. Any strategy in respect of the development of that region must be related to the establishment of secondary industries as well. First of all, it must be geared to the development of our renewable resources, our great timberlands, which so richly endow our region. The type of industry referred to will again require people.
It is not necessary to elaborate on the importance the development of these industries will have in helping alleviate the unemployment crisis in Canada. Furthermore, an immediate result would be a great increase in tourist traffic, an industry of prime importance to that area. A traffic survey carried out by the Department of Public Works underlines this statement. As members of this House well know, a great number of our neighbours to the south use this road link in travelling to the state of Alaska. The people visiting our country, who share with us its vastness and its beauty in that area, take nothing home with them but memories of a unique adventure and pictures which they might have taken en route. However, they are contributing to the western economy to an extent that the tourist industry ranks second only in importance in our area.
The bill proposes the establishment of an authority that could act on behalf of our government in discussions with the United States, which has indicated its great interest in this endeavour. I am referring in particular to discussions held with that country regarding the sharing of costs. The authority could also represent our government in discussions with officials from areas and regions bordering the highway, such as officials of the province of British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
I have lived in that area and I have been involved in the service and tourist industry for the last 20 years, so I know a little about the highway in question. If we are concerned about northern development, it is essential that we develop a transportation policy and a road strategy, which does not exist in Canada today, and it would help if the proposed authority could develop this strategy and a general philosophy concerning northern highway travel. Many people who live in the north and many leaders up there have voiced a need for such a strategy. In fact, some of the people living up there will have to take a stand soon. They will have to tell us soon that there should be no more construction of roads, highways and road links in northern Canada until a philosophy is developed and we protect the way of life which they have valued for so many years. So far as our native people are concerned, the first wars in Canada against our natives were fought over roads and railroads, the iron horse that traverses our country.
When we go up to our last frontier, we find that we have built the Mackenzie Highway, the Dempster Highway and now we are completing the Alaska Highway without any over-all plan, strategy or philosophy. In this bill I am proposing that we establish such a plan. I can visualize the highway and the commission developing a highway system with proper campsites for tourists to enjoy. Every 75 or 80 miles there would be an airstrip which would contribute to the safety and comfort of the people travel-
Alaska-Yukon Highway Authority
ling on the highway and which could be used in emergency cases, because highway accidents do occur. I live there, and I know.
The commission could develop rest areas where people could stay for a day or two, visit with the people who live in the area and share their dreams. They could go home with rich memories. We could establish parks along the highway and negotiate with provincial and territorial governments for those things that we hold so dear. I would like hon. members to share with me for a moment a picture of what it would be like 100 years from now-and I am only dreaming-if we could develop this area. Perhaps we could have on each side of the highway a park reaching out 1,000 miles, and we could compare the benefits of that park in perhaps 50 or 100 years with what we would have if industry and commerce, with no proper control, were to clutter up the highway.
The commission could take into account the provision of special facilities for the maintenance and establishment of new tourist facilities. It could ensure that the necessary amenities are provided to ensure the safety and comfort of tourists. In other words, the bill would ensure that those of us who have pioneered on the last frontier may have some input into plans which are normally worked out by people who are not familiar with the area and are certainly not familiar with the dreams and ambitions of the local citizens, nor the dangers involved in carrying out such ambitious plans-dangers to the environment and ecology as well as to the native people who have lived there for so many years. They will be speaking out, and if they do not remember to do so I will remind them that if we carry on with a northern development concept such as the one we are embarking upon right now, without giving further thought to it, then indeed we will have spoiled our last chance to do something different for once.
The urgency of the Alaska Highway construction has been recognized by all governments affected by the route and they have made submissions to the federal government expressing their concern. The Alaska, Yukon and British Columbia Chambers of Commerce have always considered the Alaska Highway to have top priority, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has included the reconstruction and paving of the highway in their policy paper and has brought it to the attention of the government. As I have said before, the government has indeed responded and some minor improvements have been carried out in the past.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the highway from Dawson Creek to Whitehorse presents today as unique a challenge as it did in 1942. In fact, it represents an even greater challenge because we must surely have recognized over the last 100 years that we cannot just blindly pursue monetary and economic gains and that we must accept our responsibility, not just to ourselves but to the people living in the area.
We have a responsibility to the rest of the world to develop at least one region on this earth in such a way that we and our children can be proud of it. I am afraid that if we do not establish a commission to supervise this task, the highway will be just another road link and another mess such as we have in northern Canada and such as existed in the early days when the settlers trav-

I therefore strongly recommend that if this bill cannot be adopted today, that at least the subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and that I be given the opportunity to bring to the committee the dream of so many northern Canadians to establish something of which we can all be proud as Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that I speak for most members in this chamber when I thank the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) for giving us an opportunity to discuss one of the most important highways in Canada, a highway about which for a number of years we have heard a great deal in the House.
The hon. member's predecessor spoke on this very subject whenever the matter arose in the House, and I remember him lobbying behind the scenes also on the subject of the Alaska Highway. In 1970, or possibly in 1971 in the last parliament the hon. member for Red Deer introduced a private member's bill dealing with the subject of the Alaska Highway. In my remarks at that time I advanced a proposition which at first glance may have appeared a bit far fetched, but I think on analysis hon. members would agree it is the key not only to getting the Alaska Highway problem solved but also to solving another major Canadian problem, namely, a better, faster link between central Canada and the Maritimes.
My proposition, which I consider sound and has a good chance of success if we can convince a few more people, involves encouraging the U.S. government to construct a four-lane, high speed highway across the top of the state of Maine, linking the eastern townships auto route with a point in New Brunswick, possibly involving some part of U. S. Interstate 95, in return for the Canadian federal government spending an equal amount of money on upgrading and paving the Alaska Highway. The arguments in favour of this proposition are obvious. It would

promote Canadian unity; it would bring Canadians closer together by reducing travelling time between central Canada and the maritimes by a minimum of five hours. I am not talking from the eastern Canadian point of view.
In addition, it would reduce transportation costs between central Canada and the maritime provinces. It would make possible a large increase in tourist traffic between the maritime provinces, central Canada and the American mid-west. Residents of Montreal and of eastern Ontario would be able to drive to P.E.I. or Nova Scotia easily in one day. This would make a great difference for tens of thousands of Canadians who now normally vacation on the coasts of Maine and New Jersey simply because they can drive there in one day.

Considering that there would be two or three times more tourists visiting the maritime provinces and that the instability of the weather in the area might bring a premature end to many seaside vacations, it can be felt that more tourists could turn to other regions of the maritimes, and also to Forillon Park, in the Gaspe Peninsula, which could certainly attract many.
I also suggest that a national park be developed along the northeast coast of New Brunswick, which would increase the movement of tourists visiting all other regions of the maritimes.

Although Maritimers may feel more exposed to Upper Canada commerce as a result of such a highway, and I suppose this might worry some people, I am confident that competitive Maritimes business operators would benefit enormously.
There are growing protests in the state of Maine about speeding Canadian tourists on their present east-west roads. These complaints about fast-driving Canadians presumably would be eliminated or reduced. An additional argument is that such a route would open up for possible exploitation and development a new national park area in the eastern townships region of Quebec along the Maine-Quebec border. This is one of the most depressed areas of Quebec, the southern Beauce region. This would be an ideal location for a national park. This kind of highway, pushing the eastern townships auto route through to the Maine border, would be a main link to the park for the 21 million people in Montreal. In effect, it would put them two hours away from another major national park. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this project would do more in economic terms for the Maritimes and Quebec than scores of past projects and programs costing ten times as much.

It could well be that, in the Gaspe Peninsula, in Rimous-ki, in eastern Quebec as well as in northern New Brunswick, some people strongly oppose the construction of such a highway.
Indeed, they could fear that it would reduce the influx of tourists in their area. They claim that the tourists would head for the beaches of P.E.I. as quickly as possible, to return home by the quickest and shortest route. According to that argument, tourism, which is their best
March 9, 1973

hope for a more prosperous future, would really take a beating.
I do not agree with that argument; I am convinced that we can reasonably hope to triple the number of tourists in the Maritimes, and that those tourists will affect the whole area, including northeastern New Brunswick and the eastern part of the Gaspe Peninsula.

Undoubtedly, some maritimers would feel that they might lose the protection against Upper Canada's commerce that is afforded them by geography. But, as I said earlier, I am confident that competitive Martimes enterprises would be in a much better position than they are now. Maritimers in general would benefit from this closer and faster road link. Presumably, some negative feelings would also exist in southern and central Maine. The argument would be that tourist traffic would be diverted away from the Maine roads which presently carry a substantial percentage of the Canadian tourists going to and returning from our maritime provinces, and Maine tourism would suffer in consequence.
Maine environmentalists are also anxious that northern Maine be preserved as a wilderness area. Here I am pinpointing the problems to be faced in implementing this kind of road project across the top of Maine. I feel that the Maine fears of losing tourism are as unjustified as northern New Brunswick and eastern Quebec fears. If you pour three times as many people into an area, by a direct route, as went there previously, they will filter back in all kinds of different ways and by different roads.
The weather down there is never certain for two weeks at a time. As I said earlier, vacations are cut short. People will come back in a variety of ways, and as a result benefit all the maritimes and Maine. The time difference that this route would make in travel between, let us say, Ottawa, Montreal or even Toronto, and P.E.I. would be anywhere from four to five hours. This is enough to make it very easy to drive from Montreal to P.E.I. in one day. It would even be possible to drive from Toronto to Prince Edward Island in one day if one did not mind driving for ten or twelve hours. The potential benefit to the Maritimes through tourism would be enormous-far greater than any program we have ever developed in that area. The question is, Mr. Speaker, how do we get this project implemented? There have been proposals regarding the Maine corridor for quite a while. In 1969, Governor Curtis of Maine approved a $30 million bond issue to build a road across the state. In 1970, this bond issue was rejected by the voters. That is where the matter stands now as far as Maine is concerned.
What I am arguing is that Canada should hold out to the American government the incentive that we would spend a lot more money on the Alaska Highway, as they want us to do, and consequently could get them to put up a substantial sum of money for the highway which I propose- in fact, get them to pay the total cost of the highway across the state of Maine. Residents of that state would be delighted to find that they did not have to pay for it.
I am convinced that the American authorities are responsive. Indeed, in the discussions I have had with
Alaska-Yukon Highway Authority
Senator Gravel and Senator Stevens of Alaska, they were most enthusiastic. I have also had discussions with several other congressmen and senators and all are responsive to the idea who have indicated that they are prepared to support it and help get it through Congress. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, congressmen and senators have the power to institute legislation, and I have a number of indications that senators and congressmen are prepared to sponsor such a bill. In their view it would have an excellent chance of success.
I have talked about the benefits to eastern Canada of such a project, and the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River has indicated the tremendous benefits that will accrue to the west. The Alaska Highway route has great tourist potential, of course, because nearly everybody wants to go to a place they have not visited before. When the Dempster Highway is finished, people will be able to go to the Arctic Ocean. With the facilities that the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River has suggested, there would be a fantastic additional tourist potential in the west.
We can accomplish something that is rather wonderful for both east and west at one time, without an enormous expenditure above what is already required for upgrading the Alaska Highway. As the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River pointed out, the complete paving of that highway is a long way off. Perhaps two or three hundred miles of it have to be rebuilt. The upgrading must come before the paving, so the completed highway is a long way off.
To get back to the project which I am proposing, I am indebted to the hon. member for having been fortunate enough to have his private member's bill drawn so early in the session. I have a motion on the order paper which reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to entering into contractual arrangements with the United States of America providing that that country should expend an amount to build a highway of inter state highway system standards through the State of Maine, one of the United States of America, connecting the province of Quebec with the Atlantic provinces in return for Canada expending an equal amount on upgrading and paving on that portion of the Alaska Highway that lies within Canada.
That motion is so far down the list that it will not be discussed in this session, so I am glad to have the opportunity to talk about it this afternoon. To implement it, we would obviously have to obtain the green light from the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick, the state of Maine and the governments of the United States and Canada. I think that if we can get the approval of Quebec, New Brunswick and Maine it should be possible to work things out with both federal governments. I certainly intend to do some additional lobbying to try to convince the provincial authorities that they will not lose by it. Some hon. members from northeastern New Brunswick and from Quebec seem to think that there will be a loss to their areas but, Mr. Speaker, every one would benefit from the Maine corridor.
Several options are available. One of the long-time promoters of the project, Mr. Douglas Fullerton, chairman of the National Capital Commission, has proposed that Canada should guarantee to Maine an immediate

March 9, 1973
Alaska-Yukon Highway Authority
throughput on a toll road across that state, but I feel this approach might entail more difficulties than the project I am suggesting. Quebec may be hesitant because of pressure in the Riviere du Loup, Rimouski and Gaspe areas. I think this could be overcome by stressing the benefits which would accrue to the depressed Beauce area. If we threw in the sweetener of additional national parks for those areas of New Brunswick and Quebec, this would help convince any remaining doubters.
I believe there is no single project that this government could support which would provide as many side benefits, for as many people, and which would be as important for the Canadian balance of tourist payments as this. It would do great things for Canadians in the west and the east, and without question it would bring us closer together.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for only very few recorded paragraphs in the somewhat long hope that we can accede to the wish of the hon. member who has brought this timely and important proposition before us for establishment of an Alaska-Yukon Highway authority. In passing, may I say that we are living in a small world. The previous speaker, I was amazed to hear, managed to go from Alaska to Maine, back to Alaska and then back to Quebec in about 20 minutes. That is a wonderful achievement and shows the importance of our transportation links.
Our country is somewhat odd. Looking at the map, one will see that Canada is topless; the country goes on and on over the pole. On the other hand, some parts of Canada extend south of northern California. Proposed highways are easy to justify if one considers our geography. I think the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has brought forward a good proposition and we favour sending his proposal to the appropriate committee. Without doubt, the north and the area for which he speaks generally is ripe for better highway links and construction. Continuing in the way we have for many years, by bits and pieces and patchwork policies, is not good enough. We need a definite planning agency in this area. In my view, that agency or authority should be set up as a Crown corporation. Of course, if this bill were referred to committee we could discuss it in greater detail.
It is wonderful how times change. I can remember how, 35 years ago, the people of Vancouver opposed the construction of a highway, and certainly of a railway link, up to the Peace River country because it was thought that building links to that area would enable the people there to leave the area and come down to Vancouver. Now the people of Vancouver and of the west are as keen as members representing central and northern parts of the country to see a responsible authority established that will help to plan, establish and promote highways such as the one the hon. member has in mind. Such a highway, I am sure, will prove the key to the development of industry and the planning of the entire area contiguous to the highway. Certainly it will lead to better relations between our country and the Americans and will be a boom for the tourist trade.
Those are my thoughts, Mr. Speaker. I hope the House will permit the bill to go to committee, as the hon. member wishes, where it can receive detailed examination.
March 9, 1973

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, without wishing to take anything from Your Honour's dignity, I think Your Honour cut short a rather pleasant occasion this afternoon when the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin) occupied the Speaker's chair. There is a lady speaker in the other place and I am wondering if this afternoon, for the first time in Canadian history, a lady acted as Speaker of this House. I congratulate her.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I realize that the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) feels strongly about those matters outlined in his bill. I have had the pleasure and opportunity of visiting the west on several occasions, and I have visited the Yukon territory. I think Canadians cannot have any idea of the size and beauty of Canada unless they have made a trip such as I did.
The Alaska Highway was built to be an important road link, mainly in the war years. The hon. member referred to its history prior to that time. When one visits the Yukon territory and stands on the shores of the Yukon River, thinks of that river's past history and what it has meant to generations gone by, one cannot help being carried away by the beauty and magnitude of Canada.
The hon. member is to be congratulated for bringing forward a measure that would, if passed, affect his region to a large degree. He has done what other hon. members of the House have done. If we, as individual members of this House, do not stand up and speak on behalf of our various regions of Canada, we will hardly form a federal parliament.
I am greatly concerned about the hon. member's proposal to set up an authority which is to be a nonCrown authority. I do not quite know what he means by a non-Crown authority, even after reading the bill. I am concerned about the matter because I feel that the Department of Public Works has for many years been downgraded by various governments, and the money which the department is permitted to spend on projects in all Canada has been reduced. Rather than establishing a separate authority to handle any project in any particular area, it is my contention that we should use the Department of Public Works as a federal agency in order to establish the federal presence everywhere in Canada. For this reason, I feel it should have the capability of making a contribution to projects such as the hon. member has mentioned.
Let us look at the past. When the Department of Public Works, with the assistance of the military, constructed the Rideau Canal it had wide powers and almost complete authority over waterways such as the Ottawa River. Some of the department's achievements, such as the canal structures in Ontario, are an important part of Canada's history. Yet today, when minor items concerning tourist projects are brought forward, so many difficulties arise that one feels rather like an athlete trying to jump over a ten-foot wall.
The Department of Public Works should be a department making a considerable financial contribution in all
Alaska-Yukon Highway Authority
regions. From talking to people who have been concerned about the Alaska Highway, I understand that a large section would need to be relocated before paving could be carried out. This involves a major construction project. I do not suppose it would be out of line with projects carried out in the past when the Department of Public Works was one of the major departments in government. That situation could return.
Not many days ago I was speaking about the Department of National Defence in the course of the debate on the budget. As we know, that department made an important contribution to the construction of the Alaska Highway in the early stages. I mentioned this in my speech. I also put forward a proposal with regard to a pioneer tourist train up the Ottawa Valley, a proposal which has received widespread support from my area, as I am sure the bill before us will be widely supported in the hon. member's region.
But, Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to get things done in connection with a suggestion of that kind. One feels like an athlete attempting to jump over a ten-foot wall. One is confronted with questions such as: Where shall we get a steam locomotive? Where are we going to find coaches? One is told, for example, that the roadbed is not firm enough. We are talking now about a fairly simple project intended to encourage the tourist industry by bringing back a semblance of the old pioneer days when the timber trade was flourishing. If a scheme like this seems difficult to realize, compare it with the relocation and paving of a large section of the Alaska Highway. Nevertheless, it is proposals such as these which all hon. members should encourage and promote with support from others.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH ALASKA-YUKON HIGHWAY AUTHORITY
speechtext:
The hon. member says he is sure getting it. I am quite prepared to back up any effort the Department of Public Works may make. I believe the department should be a major factor in carrying out many of these projects. But it has been downgraded financially for the past several decades. I believe it should be restored to the position it held at the turn of the century. I am not criticizing the hon. member's proposal; I am simply taking it by another route. I am saying it would be good for the unity of Canada if it were done from Ottawa by a federal department in close liaison with the local authorities.
I am concerned by the recommendation in the bill that three Members of Parliament be appointed to the corporation which is envisaged to carry out the hon. member's plan. I am even more concerned when I see that the three Members recommended in the bill are members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. A number of bills have been brought forward in the last few years seeking to have Members of Parliament appointed to the boards of Crown corporations or agencies. All of them were talked out, no matter which government was in power at the time. I would be somewhat afraid that the presence of three members of the opposition on such an important body might jeopardize the project, rather than assist it. That is why I should like to see the work sponsored by the Department of Public Works, since that department involves all members of this House.
